doc.title: Ruth Lion interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

chapter: Alfred Lion and the founding of Blue Note
title: Why Alfred was drawn to African American music
summary: She sees it as love of the music's expression rather than a mission; Frank Wolff's view is that blues, soul and religiosity underlie it.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: We talked a little bit on the phone a couple of times about what it was about African American musicians especially that seemed to attract him. Do you feel that it was a mission for him to promote their music and record it? Or what was it?

I think it was that he was so interested in that particular musical expression. And I don’t know that it was actually a mission any more than it was just something that he wanted to hear, and he wanted to — whoever else might want to hear it he’d like to give it to them. He was a very giving person. And I think that’s what it was. And he couldn’t hear enough of that music, you know, to please himself. So then he would go ahead and record these musicians. It was like Frank, his associate, put it in this way. The blues were always the basis of everything. And maybe the blues could be rhythmic and all, but there was always that sort of certain undercurrent of soul or religiosity, something of that sort that he would hear. And both Frank and Alfred were religious people. So that — the music was like for them, an expression of their own souls. So yes, he did record a number of non-African American artists. But they were artists who had that, what he was listening for.

That’s so hard to pin down, but saying in the same sentence “soul” and “blues” and “religious feeling,” that makes a lot of sense to me, that it just — every one of those things has a certain thing that touches you in your heart, and obviously that this music just wouldn’t let him go, right? He had to do this.
He had to. He really did.
